newsitem.title: USA: Accused World Trade bomber helped entering USA - agent.
newsitem.headline: Accused World Trade bomber helped entering USA - agent.

text.p: The accused mastermind of the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing claimed to have received help from the Iraqi consulate when he boarded a plane bound for New York without a visa, a federal agent testified on Monday.

Immigration and Naturalisation Service agent Mark Cosine said Ramzi Yousef arrived from Pakistan on a Pakistan Airlines flight at Kennedy International Airport on Sept. 1, 1992 and asked for political asylum.

Yousef, a Moslem militant, is on trial in federal court for allegedly building and planting the bomb that exploded in an underground parking garage at the World Trade Centre on Feb. 26, 1993. His alleged accomplice Eyad Ismoil is accused of driving the van that carried the bomb.
The blast at the famous 110-story twin towers killed six people, injured more than 1,000 and caused more than $550 million in damage.
Prosecutors say Yousef and Ismoil are part of a war of terrorism against the United States to retaliate for U.S. support for Israel.
Yousef was one of five people on the 1992 Pakistan flight stopped by U.S. authorities because of questionable documents, Cosine testified.
Yousef told the INS agent at the time that he had received help from the Iraqi consulate in boarding the plane.
"I asked him how he got on the flight without the visa. He said he had a brother in the Iraqi consulate who helped him get on the aircraft," Cosine testified.

Also on that flight was Ahmed Ajaj, a Pakistan Airlines employee testified last week. Ajaj was one of four other Moslem fundamentalists convicted in a 1994 trial of the World Trade Centre bombing. Yousef's trial was delayed because he fled the country.
Ajaj, a Palestinian born in Jerusalem, was detained after trying to enter the United States with a forged Swedish passport.
Cosine testified that Ajaj carried a suitcase of bombing manuals and audio and video tapes in Arabic that dealt with explosives, guns and weaponry.
At the 1994 trial, an FBI fingerprint expert testified that Yousef's prints were found on Ajaj's bomb manuals.
The immigration officer testified that Yousef also carried an array of forged documents.
Yousef and Ismoil fled the country the night of the explosion, and both men were brought back to the United States in 1995. Yousef was captured in Pakistan, and Ismoil was arrested in Jordan.
